etymologies.etymologyHTML: From Late Middle English paissaunt, from Anglo-Norman paisant, from Old French païsant, païsan (“countryman, peasant”), from païs (“country”), from Latin pāgus (“district”) + Old French -enc (“member of”), from Frankish -inc, -ing "-ing"; which was an alteration of earlier Late Latin pāgēnsis (“inhabitant of a district”). Doublet of paisano.

definitions.definition: A member of the lowly social class that toils on the land, constituted by small farmers and tenants, sharecroppers, farmhands and other laborers on the land where they form the main labor force in agriculture and horticulture.

quote.citation: 1986, Martin Kitchen, British Policy Towards the Soviet Union during the Second World War‎[1], Palgrave Macmillan, →ISBN, →OCLC, →OL, page 137:
quote.text: The Ambassador warned him of the consequences if his mission to Moscow were a failure, both to Churchill's position at home and to Russia's prospects in the war. He insisted that he should not allow himself to be offended 'by a peasant who didn't know any better'. Churchill listened in silence, then returned to the dacha leaving Clark Kerr outside.

definitions.definition: (derogatory) An uncouth, crude or ill-bred person.
(attributive) Characteristic of or relating to a peasant or peasants; unsophisticated.

quote.citation: 2007, Brad Bird, Ratatouille, spoken by Colette
quote.text: Ratatouille? It's a peasant dish. Are you sure you want to serve this to Ego?

quote.citation: c. 1599–1602 (date written), William Shakespeare, “The Tragedie of Hamlet, Prince of Denmarke”, in Mr. William Shakespeares Comedies, Histories, & Tragedies […] (First Folio), London:  […]  Isaac Iaggard, and Ed[ward] Blount, published 1623, →OCLC, [Act II, scene ii], line 520:
